projections.plain_pitch: A small 96x96 tile world with honest little physics: heat spreads, water flows, plants grow, things wear out. Tribes of 6 to 30 agents live in it, and every single thing an agent does is a short program written in a made-up 40-instruction mini-language — move, look, take, put, hit, heat, wait, count, if, loop. There is no hand-written AI. Every night a piece of software reads all the programs that worked that day, finds the chunk of code that keeps repeating, and gives that chunk a name; that name becomes a new instruction, and "technology" in this project means exactly that growing list of named chunks — nothing else. Ashcairn on its own is the library and nothing but the library: there are no buildings, no map full of kilns, no structures on the ground. Buildings are Glyphworks, which is the same engine with a "put the invention in the landscape" layer bolted on top. Strip that away and Ashcairn is a text file of named subroutines that grows, plus a survival economy that kills the ones that cost too much to run.
projections.how_it_invents_plain:
Here is one invention, end to end. During the day, the world says "this agent is cold". The system brute-forces combinations of instructions until it finds a program that fixes it — literally trying sequences, shortest first, and running each one in a fast little virtual machine to see if it works. Three agents in three tribes each solve cold-ness today, and by chance all their winning programs contain the same nine-instruction run: look for the nearest wood, walk there, pick it up, walk to the fire, drop it. Across the whole day's pile of successful programs, that same run shows up forty times.

At night the compressor (a real, fast, off-the-shelf Rust tool called Stitch) scans that whole pile looking for the repeated chunk that would delete the most total code if you replaced every copy with a single call. This one wins: forty copies, eight instructions saved each time. So it gets promoted to instruction #41. A small language model on the laptop writes it a name and one line of description — `feed_fire`, "fetch the nearest fuel and add it to a fire" — and it goes in the library with a date, an inventor, and a list of its parts.

Next morning the brute-force search treats `feed_fire` as one single move. A task that would have needed a fourteen-step program yesterday now needs six, and six is inside the budget, so it gets solved for the first time ever. That new solution goes into tonight's pile, and can itself become part of tomorrow's named chunk. That is the entire compounding loop. It is not a metaphor and there is no magic in it — it is repeated-substring detection over code, run once a night, with the wins fed back into tomorrow's search. One extra bit: when brute force fails on the same task N nights running, a 4-billion-parameter language model on your GPU writes a rough program with blanks in it and the search fills the blanks. That's the only place a model's opinion enters, and it's checked by actually running it, so it can't lie to you.
projections.month6_screen:
A single card, headed something like `NIGHT 174 · 3 TRIBES · LIB 58`.

Under it, the honest thing: four mornings out of five, a line saying no abstraction cleared the bit threshold last night. Nothing new. On the fifth morning there is a card: a name like `stack_then_haul`, a one-line description written by the small model ("gather items into a pile, then carry the pile"), "bits saved: 190", three parent functions listed as breadcrumbs, and a six-line body you can actually read, because compressed things are short by definition.

Below that, two sparklines. LIBRARY DEPTH: a step up to 2 around week two, a step to 3 around week five, a step to 4 around week eight, then a flat line for the last four months. CALORIES PER SOLVED TASK: a satisfying steep fall for six weeks, then a shallow drift that could be noise. Tap through and you get the family tree of the library, which has not meaningfully changed shape since about week nine, and a button to replay any program in your browser, which still works and is still nice.

You look at it for four seconds. Most mornings there is nothing to see.
projections.month6_invented_examples:
Realistic case, not best case. Roughly 40 to 80 named things total, and honestly maybe a dozen you would call meaningful.

1. `take_nearest(x)` — go to the closest x and pick it up. Week 1. Boring, three instructions, and underneath about 60% of everything else. This one is genuinely good and you will be fond of it.
2. `feed_fire` — fetch fuel, put it on the fire. Week 1-2.
3. `bank_the_fire` — damp the fire down so it survives unattended. Week 3-ish, contains `feed_fire`, so it is depth 2. This is the first one that feels like a real practice.
4. `haul_pair` — two agents carry one heavy thing together. Only exists because you gave the mini-language a `carry_with` instruction, so it's less of a discovery than it looks.
5. `winter_cache` — repeat "take food, put in store" until the store count hits N. Around week five, depth 3. Realistically your high-water mark for "reads like a practice".
6. `overwinter` — literally `winter_cache` then `bank_the_fire` then huddle. Depth 4, arrives around week eight, looks like the most impressive thing in the library, and is three older names in a row with nothing new inside it. This is the exact shape of what month 6 keeps producing.
7. `forage_pass` — the model's dignified name for "sense; if present, take". Three instructions of plumbing. It compresses brilliantly because it appears 900 times, which is precisely why it gets minted. Roughly three in four of your abstractions are this kind of thing: positional plumbing with a good name.
8. `secure_the_ground` — you will not be able to say what this one does even after reading it. It is a repeated code pattern with no human meaning, christened confidently by a 4B model. The naming step is the least trustworthy component in the whole system and the most persuasive-looking output.

What you will NOT have: anything like `repeat_until_stable(f)` or `teach(f, learner)` — a named chunk that takes another named chunk as an argument. The design doc promises these as the month 3-6 payoff and the audit calls that fantasy, flatly, for a mechanical reason: the compressor finds repeated code patterns with plain blanks in them. It does not invent the concept of "a function that takes a function". To get one you'd have to add first-class functions to the mini-language AND hand-write several examples of the pattern first — at which point you authored it and it isn't a discovery. Same for the "wildest plausible" endgame, an invented apprenticeship protocol. That is not going to happen. Believe the audit here; the design doc is selling you something its own compressor cannot do.
projections.reaches_technology:
No. Not close, and it is worth being blunt about why.

Fire is not discovered — `heat` is one of the forty instructions you wrote on Saturday. Houses do not exist at all; there is no building in Ashcairn (that is Glyphworks, and it is a different and harder project). Tools exist only as far as your forty instructions can express them. The design doc says this itself, in its own honest-ceiling section: if the forty primitives cannot express chemistry, no amount of compression will invent chemistry. That sentence is the whole answer. The ceiling isn't the compressor, it's the vocabulary you hand-write on day one, plus how many genuinely different problems a 96x96 survival world can pose. The audit puts that at eight to fifteen distinct families of behaviour.

Where the doc and the audit disagree, the gap is large and you should believe the audit. Doc: 300-800 named things, depth 8-12, six months of compounding. Audit: 30-80 named things, depth 3-4, real compounding for about eight weeks. That is not a rounding difference — it's "a civilization" versus "a decent vocabulary".

So yes, the civilization framing is a costume. Underneath it, honestly described, this is an automatic refactoring tool for a tribe of little robots, wrapped in a survival economy that kills refactors that cost too much to run. The real endpoint is: a system that teaches itself a good, short, readable vocabulary for one small world, and can prove it did so, in bits.

But do not throw it out on that basis, because the flip side is real and rare. Of the whole pile of ideas this came from, Ashcairn has the lowest risk of being secretly authored by you. Nothing about `bank_the_fire` was written by a designer — it was carved out of behaviour that kept agents alive, and it has a date and a parts list. And there is almost no risk of it producing convincing nonsense, because programs either run or they don't and the virtual machine cannot be sweet-talked. Bad output here looks like a boring abstraction, not a fake one. That is a genuinely unusual property and it is the actual reason to build this.

Two mechanisms in it are also properly clever and worth keeping whatever you build. First, the teaching bottleneck: only K functions can be demonstrated to the next generation each season, so a big library is a liability for a small tribe, and lean well-compressed tribes beat hoarders. Watching a tribe refactor its own knowledge for teachability is a real, counter-intuitive thing you cannot fake. Second, the multi-world test: run several worlds with different rules and let a wanderer carry at most five functions across. A function that still works in a differently-generated world is proof the idea was real and not just overfitted to one map. The audit says that should be promoted from a nightly check to your main source of training data, and it's right.
projections.honest_month6_feeling:
Week 2 is genuinely thrilling. Something you did not write appeared with a name on it, and today's search used it to reach further than yesterday's. That feeling is real and it is why this idea keeps getting recommended.

Month 6 is a different job. By then you are not watching a civilization, you are maintaining a search system. Most nights nothing clears the threshold. Your evening question stops being "what did they invent" and becomes "should the bit threshold be 40 or 25", which is a parameter you will move up and down for weeks without ever knowing the right answer, because there isn't one. The design doc offers an "optional weekly five-minute nudge" where you read the unsolved-task list and hand-write a task. By month 6 that is not optional and it is not five minutes — it is the only thing still generating new material, and you will feel that you are the engine and the compressor is the flywheel.

There is also a hard fork in month 1 that the doc soft-pedals. The thing that decides how deep the search can reach is the guide that tells it which instruction to try next. The doc plans to start with a dumb statistical guide (basically "after `move`, `take` is common") and upgrade later if needed. The audit says that dumb guide gives essentially no help over a growing library and stalls you at depth 2-3, so you will be building a small neural network to guide the search in month one, not month five. Treat that as the plan. It is a proper machine-learning engineering job, and it is where a browser-game builder either discovers he loves this or discovers he is doing homework. Worse, the audit points out the training data for that network is thin — replaying against one small world just teaches it that world's quirks, which is the opposite of what you need.

The nicest true thing the doc says about month 6: you will read the little mini-language fluently, like a language. That happens. It's a real pleasure and it lasts.
projections.best_moment:
Sunday afternoon of the first weekend, and this is not a maybe — across the whole pool of ideas this one has the most reliable early payoff. Saturday you write the mini-language, the virtual machine, forty instructions, six hardcoded tasks, and a plain brute-force search. Sunday you `pip install stitch_core`, hand it the day's winning programs, and print the top result. A subroutine you never wrote comes back with a name and a bit count. Then you re-run Monday's search and watch it solve something it could not reach the day before, specifically because that name now exists. Forty-eight hours, no ambiguity, measured in a number.

Second-best moment, weeks four to six: the first named chunk whose body contains two other named chunks that were themselves invented. It is a small line on a graph and it will feel much bigger than that, because it is the first evidence the thing stacks rather than just accumulates.

Third, if you build the teaching bottleneck: the first time a small tribe with a lean library outcompetes a hoarder because it can actually teach what it knows. Weeks six to twelve. That one you'll want to tell people about.
projections.worst_moment:
Two candidates, and you'll probably hit both.

The early one, around week three or four: you realise the dumb search guide isn't guiding anything, depth has stuck at 2, and to go further you need to write a neural network. That's a genre change from game dev to ML engineering, several weeks long, with no visible progress on the phone card while you do it.

The real one, weeks eight to twelve: the compressor starts coming back empty most nights. Not broken — just done. It has already found everything that recurs in a world with about a dozen kinds of problem in it, and the remaining repeated patterns are below threshold or meaningless. You lower the threshold and get plumbing with grand names. You raise it and get nothing. You start hand-writing tasks to keep it moving, which works, and each one you write is a small admission that you are now the source of novelty. That is the point where most people quietly stop opening the app.

There's a third, sneakier one worth flagging because the design doc has it exactly backwards. The doc's proudest line is that compression IS metabolism — that shorter code and fewer calories are the same objective, "the single most elegant coupling in this document". The audit calls it a category error and it's right: the compressor minimises how much CODE there is, not how long it takes to RUN. A four-instruction abstraction can spin 40,000 steps in a loop. So the compressor will happily mint short, expensive names, and your survival selection will then starve the tribes that use them. The two halves of your engine will quietly fight each other, and it'll look like a mysterious balance problem rather than a design flaw. Fix it before you notice it: before admitting any abstraction, re-rank the compressor's candidates by how many actual execution steps they save across the whole day's programs, not by how many characters. That's a small change and it is load-bearing.
projections.who_should_pick_it: The right person for this is someone who wants a small, provable machine that visibly teaches itself a vocabulary within 48 hours and never leaves you wondering whether it's working — and who will be genuinely satisfied with an excellent two-month project rather than resentful that it isn't a civilization.
projections.jargon_decoder:
DSL ("SURV") — the made-up 40-instruction mini-language the agents' behaviour is written in; think of it as a tiny assembly language you invented for one game.

LAMBDA ABSTRACTION — a named chunk of that code with a blank or two in it, i.e. a function. "A library of named lambda abstractions" just means "a list of subroutines with names".

MDL / "compression gain" / "bits saved" — how much shorter the whole day's pile of code gets if you replace every copy of a repeated chunk with one call to a new name. A bigger number means a more useful chunk. It is literally a number going up.

ENUMERATIVE SEARCH — brute force. Try every combination of instructions, shortest first, run each one, keep what works. No cleverness, just a lot of tries.

WAKE-SLEEP — the day/night rhythm. Day: solve problems by brute force. Night: compress what worked into new names, and practise with them. That's all the phrase means.

LEARNED PRIOR / "search prior" — the hint system that tells brute force which instruction to try next so it doesn't waste time. The doc plans a dumb one and hopes; the audit says you'll need to build a small neural network here in month one.

HIGHER-ORDER ABSTRACTION — a subroutine that takes another subroutine as an input, like `do_until_it_stops_changing(f)`. The doc promises these as the big payoff; the audit says the compressor cannot produce them, full stop.

TRANSMISSION BOTTLENECK — only K subroutines can be taught to the next generation each season, so knowing too much is a real disadvantage for a small tribe. This is the best idea in the document.
projections.name: Ashcairn

projections.plain_pitch:
A little valley full of stick-figure people who can only act by running tiny programs. Every simulated night, the computer brute-force searches for programs that keep them alive, then looks at the winning programs, spots chunks that keep repeating, and saves those chunks as named shortcuts. Glyphworks adds one thing on top: some of those saved chunks get turned into actual buildings standing on actual map tiles, and once a building exists, running that chunk near it costs about an eighth as much — so programs that were too expensive for the search to ever find suddenly become findable. The result you look at is a map of a valley that slowly fills with buildings you did not design.

The thing you must be clear-eyed about before anything else: Glyphworks is not a project. It is a second project bolted onto a first one. The first one is Emberlisp — the physics, the little language, the search, the compressor, the naming — and that is weeks of work before a single building exists. Glyphworks is the sequel. You cannot start at the sequel.
projections.how_it_invents_plain:
Here is the whole machine, with no vocabulary in the way.

There are about 14 materials. A material is just a row of numbers: hardness 7, moisture 0.3, ignition temperature 300, and so on. There are about 12 rules that change those numbers. "If you hit thing A with thing B hard enough and B contains pyrite, emit a spark." "If a thing's temperature goes above its ignition temperature, rewrite its numbers to the burnt version." That's the entire world. There is no such object as "fire" and no such object as "axe" anywhere in the code.

People act by running programs in a tiny language with about 28 commands: move, gather, hold, strike, heat, bind, grind, soak, if, repeat. Each night the machine picks a goal ("body temperature above 36 at night") and blindly tries millions of program combinations until something satisfies it. That's the invention. It is brute-force trying things, with clever pruning so it doesn't retry programs that behave identically to ones it already tried.

Then the compressor runs. It reads every program that worked, notices "these 14 different programs all contain the same five steps in a row," and saves those five steps as a new single command. A small language model on your GPU reads the five steps and names it, so `fn_31` becomes `bank-the-coals`. That naming is where nearly all the emotional payoff comes from, and it is also the part of the pipeline with the least actual understanding behind it. Hold that thought.

Now Glyphworks' bit. A worked example, start to finish:

Night 40. The search has been solving cold-night problems. Fourteen surviving programs contain the same run of steps: go to site 212, pile dry moss, strike flint on pyrite, repeat until it catches, add the split log, bank the ash over it. The compressor spots it and saves it as one command. The language model names it `bank-the-coals`.

Then Glyphworks runs an extra check that Emberlisp doesn't have. Two questions. First: does this chunk always happen at one fixed spot on the map, rather than wherever the person happens to be standing? Yes — every use is at site 212. Second: is it expensive to run? Yes, it burns a lot of search budget. Both yes means it gets promoted to a building plan.

The build cost is worked out by a lookup table you wrote by hand: the chunk mentions heating a lot, so it needs heat-resistant stone; if it had mentioned water it would need digging. A new goal quietly enters the nightly list: "construct this thing at site 212." The people go and build it. It takes them materials and days.

Now a building exists at site 212 with a name and a little glyph on your map. Two things changed. One, running `bank-the-coals` at site 212 now costs one eighth of what it cost before, so the search can afford to wrap other stuff around it — programs that were over budget last week are in budget this week, and new solutions pop out. Two, and this is the genuinely good idea: the building can hold a physical state that a person's hands cannot. A hearth holds temperature steady for eight hours; the bare `heat` command never could. So there are regions of the number-space — clay that has been at 800 degrees for six hours — that were literally unreachable before and are reachable now. Not cheaper. Reachable.

Those new solutions go into tomorrow's compressor pass. Some of those chunks become buildings. Some of those buildings need materials only another building can make. That's the loop, and it's a real loop, not a metaphor.

The map you look at is the state of that loop.
projections.month6_screen:
A valley drawn in canvas 2D, phone-sized. Blue river snaking down the middle. Grey-brown tiles. Maybe forty little dots for people, mostly bunched in two clumps.

Roughly ninety to a hundred and ten small glyphs scattered across it — the buildings. About fifteen of them are in grey: ruins, from a flood in month three that took out the lower terrace. You'll notice they're clustered in a stripe, because the river moved.

One line of text above it:

`NIGHT 512 · POP 38 · WORKS 97 (+1) · LIB 240`

Three event lines below it. On a random morning in month 6 they read something like:

`built ashcradle-VII at site 088`
`abandoned reedpit-III (upkeep unpaid, 41 nights idle)`
`spatial entropy dropped — cluster at 210-215`

You tap `ashcradle-VII`. It shows you its stored chunk of program, its parent chunks, its build date, how many times it's been called. And here is the honest bit: its stored chunk is `ashcradle` with two steps reordered and one material swapped, because site 088 has different stone. It is the seventh of its kind. It has a distinct glyph and a distinct name and it is not a new idea.

That's the morning. Twenty seconds. Pleasant. Then you go to work.

The good version of this morning happens maybe once every ten days by month 6: the `+1` is a kind you haven't seen, and the notification that woke you at dawn was the loud one — a building whose materials could only have been made by another building.
projections.month6_invented_examples:
Names here are invented by a 4-billion-parameter language model reading the chunk of program, so they will be kebab-case and slightly overwrought. That's genuinely charming for about six weeks.

`ash-cradle` — a hearth. Holds temperature overnight. This is the real one. It changes what's physically reachable and everything else stands on it. Arrives somewhere in week 3 to 8, depending how long the search engine fought you.

`sear-bench` — heat-treating stone to raise its hardness number so grinding it produces an edge. Second storey. Also real. This is "stone tools," except nobody wrote the word.

`reed-drier` — a rack that makes the drying rule cheap at one spot. Used constantly, saves the tribe a lot of time, is not in any meaningful sense an invention. Most of your buildings will be this.

`clay-throat` — a kiln that needs the sustained heat only an `ash-cradle` can supply. This is the second-order one, the loud notification, the "industry threshold." It may well arrive. It may also not, and the design's own cited research does not actually predict that it will — that paper found self-sustaining chains in randomly generated networks, which says nothing about whether your twelve hand-written rules contain one.

`ash-cradle-of-the-low-water` / `ash-cradle-VII` / `warmstone-nest` — the same hearth, at a different site, with one material substituted because that site has different stone. Three different glyphs. Three different names. One idea. By month 6 this category is the majority of everything the map contains.

`bind-soak-post` — a chunk the compressor liked for reasons that were purely about repeated text, not meaning. Got promoted, got built, got called four times, decayed, is now grey. A junk building. The good news, and this is the design's single best feature, is that you can see it's junk at a glance.

`grind-hearth-station` — two known chunks called together, promoted because calling them together was common. Sounds like a factory. Is a shortcut.

`third-storey-something` — pressure vessels, or fermentation, or whatever the next physics rule opens. This appears in month 4 or 5 only because you sat down one Sunday and wrote a new rule by hand. It will not appear otherwise.

Read that list honestly and you get the shape: two or three real ones, one maybe, and then variations.
projections.reaches_technology:
Partly, and then it stops in a specific place.

It genuinely does cavemen → sparks → a fire that stays lit → heat-treated stone with an edge → fired clay. That's three or four real steps up, and it's more than the version without buildings gets, because buildings reach physical states hands can't. That part of the pitch is true and the audit backs it.

But here's the thing the pitch talks around and the audit says flatly. It goes up in storeys, and you author how many storeys exist. Each "new regime" — sustained heat, then pressure, then whatever — is you loosening one guard condition in your twelve rules by hand. Twelve rules gets you roughly three to five qualitative storeys total. Each one takes a few weeks to climb. Then that's the building.

So the honest endpoint is: a valley with a hundred buildings, three or four real technological levels deep, and a ceiling made of a rule set you wrote in a weekend.

The pitch reaches for Kauffman's "adjacent possible" — the idea that each new thing you make expands what you can make next, forever. The audit calls this oversold and is right. That idea needs combination to produce genuinely new basic ingredients. What happens here is that combination produces cached shortcuts over a fixed set of rules. Cheaper and reachable-in-new-corners, yes. New ingredients, no. The design's own honest paragraph admits this; the headline paragraph doesn't.

Is the civilization framing a costume? Not entirely — I don't want to be unfair. The buildings do change the physics reachable at a location, the maintenance economy is a real selection pressure that most simulations don't model, and nobody wrote a tech tree. That's all genuine.

But strip it back and what you built is: a program search engine that caches expensive subroutines at map coordinates, plus a small language model that gives the caches names and emoji. The civilization is the presentation layer over that. It's an honest and rather beautiful presentation layer. It is still the presentation layer.

Real endpoint, in one sentence: you will build a very good, very hard search engine, and get a gorgeous six-month time-lapse of a valley filling with buildings, and roughly six to ten weeks of that period will contain things that surprise you.
projections.honest_month6_feeling:
Week 2 you are not watching anything. You are debugging. This is important and I'll come back to it.

The real week 2 feeling — say week 8, first time it's all running — is fantastic. A building appears on your map that you didn't design, with a name you didn't write, and you can watch the search behave differently around it. That is a legitimately great feeling and you'd be right to want it.

Month 6 is a different animal. Three things are true at once.

The check-in is pleasant and shallow. Twenty seconds with coffee, like watering a plant. You'll keep doing it for a year, honestly, because the map is nice and it costs nothing. But it stops being news. You'll be able to predict what today's `+1` is before you look.

You are tuning. Specifically: the threshold that decides which chunks become buildings (too loose and the map fills with junk sheds, too tight and nothing gets built), and how often the river floods (floods are your designed antidote to the tribe getting comfortable and lazy, and the frequency has to be right). The design calls this "one real chore, tuned in the first month." Believe the pattern, not the timeline — that dial gets touched all year, because what "good" means changes as the library grows.

And the only lever that actually produces new kinds is you, by hand, writing another physics rule. That's the honest month-6 loop: once every few weeks you sit down, add a rule that opens a new regime, and the built stack grows a storey over the following fortnight. It works. It's fun. It is also unmistakably you feeding the thing, not it feeding itself.

So: is it still exciting? No. Is it still good? Yes, in the way a long-running project you're proud of is good, not in the way month one is good. The audit's phrase for what month 6 produces is worth quoting because it's exactly right: quantitative sprawl that photographs beautifully and means nothing.

What you're actually doing with your time by month 6, if you're honest: occasional performance work on the search, tuning two dials, adding a physics rule now and then, and showing people the time-lapse.
projections.best_moment:
The first building you didn't design.

It's a specific, sharp moment and it's genuinely worth chasing. A push notification at dawn. The compressor found a chunk, decided it was pinned to one place and expensive, turned it into a plan, the tribe spent four days gathering stone and built it. The language model named it. It's standing on your map with a glyph. And then — this is the part that makes it more than a cosmetic — you watch a goal that was failing at ten million tries succeed at two hundred thousand, purely because that building exists.

You wrote none of those words and you did not choose that building.

The design says night 50. Realistically week 6 to 10, because the first month or two goes to the search engine, not the watching.

The second-best moment, and it may not come: the loud notification. A building whose materials could only have been made by another building. That's the line between tools and industry and the design is right that it deserves its own alert sound.
projections.worst_moment:
Weeks 2 through 6, and it's not a motivation problem. It's a bug you cannot see.

Here's what happens. The search saves work by remembering "I already tried a program that behaves exactly like this one, skip it." That memory is the only reason the search is affordable at all. But in Glyphworks, "how a program behaves" depends on which buildings are within reach, because buildings change costs and unlock physics. So the memory has to be filed by location context, and the design says so: key each remembered program by which buildings are nearby.

The design presents that as a filing problem. The audit says it's actually a stale-cache problem, and the audit is right. Buildings get built. Buildings decay. Buildings burn down in raids and drown in floods. So the context at a site changes underneath entries you already filed. The moment that happens you have two failure modes. Either you keep memories in separate boxes for every combination and your RAM disappears — 64GB, gone, fast. Or you share boxes you shouldn't, and the search quietly returns programs that are wrong at that site.

Wrong. Not crashed. No stack trace. No error. Your civilization just gets slightly stupid and you have no idea why, and finding out means instrumenting a search that expands millions of nodes a night.

This is the single hardest piece of the whole design and the audit says the first month is the search engine, possibly the first two. That is a month of work with no map, no buildings, no names, no notifications, and no dopamine. For someone whose whole craft is ship-debug-see-it-work in a browser, that month is the thing that kills this project. The fix, if you want it written down: give every site an epoch number that bumps whenever a building goes up or falls down, and treat every memory entry as valid only within its epoch.

There's also a second, softer failure around month 4. Everything works, the notifications keep arriving, and they're all the seventh kiln. Nothing is broken. It's just done being interesting and you have to decide whether adding physics rules by hand forever is a hobby you want.

One more thing on scale of effort, since you asked how much the buildings layer costs on top. The fun part — the buildings table, the cost override at a site, the promote-to-blueprint check, the map view — is genuinely two or three good weekends and it's the part you'd enjoy. The unfun part is the search rewrite, and it roughly doubles the total engine work while being harder than everything in Emberlisp combined. Emberlisp's own audit already warns you'll spend more time on the search than on the world, and that Python will be too slow by week one so you're porting the hot loop to Rust. Glyphworks multiplies that same problem by the number of distinct building contexts in play.

And two seams where your taste sneaks back in, which you should know about before you tell yourself nobody authored the tech tree. The promote-to-building check is a rule you write, and you'll tune it until it builds the things you were hoping for. And the "chunk mentions heating, so it needs heat-resistant stone" table is a hand-written price list. It's small, it isn't a tech tree, but you are the one deciding what a kiln costs, and therefore which stacks are affordable.
projections.who_should_pick_it: Someone who actively wants a hard systems-engineering problem — building a fast search with a per-location cache — and would be satisfied by a beautiful, legible map as the payoff, rather than someone who wants to watch a civilization keep surprising them.
projections.jargon_decoder:
MDL — "the shortest way to write it down wins." The compressor scores a repeated chunk by how much total text it saves across all the programs. Nothing to do with meaning.

DSL — just "the little programming language the people in the sim act in." About 28 commands: move, gather, strike, heat, bind, if, repeat.

Wake-sleep — the nightly cycle. Wake: search for programs that solve today's problems. Sleep: run the compressor over what worked and save the repeated chunks as named shortcuts. Glyphworks adds a third step: turn some of those shortcuts into buildings.

Stationarity (as used here) — nothing statistical, despite the word. It literally means "does this chunk of program always happen at one fixed spot on the map." If yes, it's a candidate for becoming a building.

Observational-equivalence bank — the memory of programs already tried, filed by what they do rather than how they're written, so the search skips duplicates. In Glyphworks this memory has to be filed by location too, and keeping it correct as buildings appear and rot is the hardest part of the project.

Adjacent possible / niche construction — the sales pitch. The claim that each thing you build expands what's buildable next, without limit. Here it's true in a small way (buildings unlock physics hands can't reach) and false in the big way the pitch implies (the twelve rules you wrote are still the ceiling).
projections.name: Glyphworks

projections.best_moment: Month 3, the domestication chart. You plot the average "yield" number of the plants growing inside a tribe's territory against the plants outside it, and the two lines pull apart and keep pulling apart. Nothing in your code says "domesticate." You wrote plants that reproduce with small random changes, and you wrote tribes that prefer eating and replanting the tastier ones, and 200 plant generations later the plants near the camps are visibly different plants. The audit calls this chart the single strongest piece of evidence in the entire document, and it's right. The wildcard that could beat it: the crop crash. Breeding for yield drags the plants' poison number down, the poison was what kept a pest off them, the pest blooms and eats the whole harvest. That is a real agricultural disaster you did not write and could not have written. If it fires, it's the best thing the project ever does. Week 1 also has a cheap, genuine thrill — the time-lapse of the empty ecosystem finding the wet ground, with no agents in it at all.
projections.worst_moment: Month 2, the day you turn on DIG. You watch. The tribes dig a hole here, a hole there, burn some stamina, wander off. No channel. Next morning, no channel. Next week, no channel. You will spend three weeks convinced this is a bug or a tuning problem, and it isn't — it's the shape of the task. To learn "dig twenty cells in a line," the tribe has to accidentally perform the entire twenty-step sequence AND then wait 300 ticks for water to arrive and yield to rise, all before it gets any signal that it did something good. Every partial attempt is strictly a loss: energy spent, nothing gained. The training method in the design is defeated by exactly this shape. The audit says so flatly and cites the benchmark that exists specifically to demonstrate it. So the worst moment is not a crash. It's month 2 through month 4 of the map staying smooth while you tell yourself it's nearly there. Runner-up: weeks 4 to 6, when every ecology run either goes extinct by day three or turns the whole map into an even green carpet, and you're hand-tuning growth rates like a man mixing paint.
projections.plain_pitch: It's a 256x256 grid world you watch like a fish tank. Every square holds a few numbers — how high the ground is, how much water and food is in the soil, how dry the brush is, what's growing there. Plants and animals each carry a little list of 16 dials (growth rate, thirst, how big a meal it makes, how poisonous it is, how far its seeds fly), and offspring inherit those dials with tiny random changes, so the wildlife genuinely evolves to fit the terrain on its own. Then you drop in small AI tribes with eight things they can do: dig, burn, plant, cull, herd, dam, fence, carry water. Everything the world ever becomes is a pattern made from those eight verbs plus whichever direction the plants' dials drift.
projections.how_it_invents_plain:
There are two engines, and they're very different in how reliable they are.

Engine one, the one that works: the tribe is the breeder. Say a tribe forages. It prefers plants with a higher "yield" dial and a lower "poison" dial, because those feed it better. That preference alone is the whole mechanism. When it eats, it's culling the low-yield plants out of the local population. When it replants seeds it was carrying, those seeds came disproportionately from the good ones. Offspring inherit the parent's 16 dials with a small random wobble. Repeat 200 generations.

Worked example. Start: wild plants near the camp average yield 1.0, poison 0.9, seed-fly-distance 12 squares. Two hundred generations of a tribe eating the tasty ones and replanting near camp, and the plants inside its territory average yield 1.8, poison 0.3, seed-fly 3. Outside the territory they're still 1.0 / 0.9 / 12. That's it. That's the invention. Literally, a cloud of numbers has drifted, and you can put the two clouds on a chart and see them separate. Nowhere in the code is there a word like "crop" or "domesticated." And the low seed-fly number is the lovely bit: seeds that stay put get replanted by the tribe, seeds that scatter don't, so the plants stop dispersing on their own — which is exactly the fingerprint archaeologists use to tell farmed grain from wild grain.

Be clear-eyed about what just happened, though. That result needs no cleverness from the AI. It needs a preference. You could hard-code the dumbest possible forager and still get the chart. It's real, it's honest, it's unauthored — and it's also basically guaranteed by construction the moment you write the selection rule. The surprise is a one-time surprise.

Engine two, the one that probably doesn't work: the tribe is a landscaper. Digging changes the height of a square, and water flows downhill, so a line of digs is an irrigation channel. The design's proudest line is that there is no "irrigation" anywhere in the code — only digging — and irrigation is a shape the AI discovers because it raises yield. That's a beautiful idea. The audit says it's the half most likely never to arrive, and explains why: a half-built channel pays worse than no channel. Twenty digs of cost, zero water, and the reward, if it ever comes, is a small yield bump five minutes of simulated time later. Trial-and-error learning cannot climb that. There's no gradient to follow — it's a cliff you either clear in one lucky leap or don't.

The audit's fix: stop making the AI find channels one dig at a time. Give it a shelf of pre-made multi-step moves — "dig a line of length N toward lower ground," "burn this patch and come back" — so building a channel is one decision instead of four hundred. That works. But be honest with yourself about the trade: at that point you authored the shape of irrigation. Not the word, and not where or whether to build one, but the shape. The pitch's cleanest claim gets quietly softened, and you should decide now whether you mind.
projections.month6_screen:
WITHOUT the landscape half (the likelier of the two):

You pick up the phone. One image, the map in false colour — greens, browns, a blue river, a few paler blotches. Over it, a hot-pink overlay showing everything that changed last night. The pink is: a few scattered burn patches near the two camps, a soft fuzzy halo around each camp where crops got replanted, and some noise along the riverbank where water moved. The overall silhouette of the map is basically what it was in month 3. No straight lines anywhere. Nothing on this map tells a stranger that anyone lives here — it just looks like healthy ground with some fire in it.

Below the map, the domestication chart. Two lines that split apart back in month 3 and have been running flat and parallel ever since, because the yield dial hit the cap you set. Below that, one headline. On a good morning it says something like "new recurring pattern detected near camp 2." You tap it. It's a burn patch shaped slightly differently from the last forty burn patches. Most mornings the headline is a false alarm from the alert system firing on a rain front.

You look for eight seconds, not thirty. You already know what it's going to say.

WITH the landscape half (you built the shelf of pre-made moves in month 3, after DIG failed):

Same map, same pink overlay, but now the silhouette has changed. Three or four dark, near-straight lines run off the river toward the flat ground — visibly not natural, visibly dug. One slope has a stack of shallow steps cut into it. A big grey burn scar from month 4 is now grassland and stays grassland. The pink overlay shows a new dig extending an old channel by six squares and a fence line going up on the north side.

Below that the domestication chart, same as above. And the headline is worth reading maybe twice a week: "upstream camp dammed the tributary, downstream yields falling." That's a war starting, and nobody wrote a war.

The difference between those two phone screens is one engineering decision you make around month 3, and the audit says it's the whole ballgame.
projections.month6_invented_examples:
Realistic case, not best case. Honest names.

1. Burn, wait, then plant. Fire adds nutrients to the soil after a delay, so a tribe that burns and comes back beats one that doesn't. This is slash-and-burn, found by accident, and it's the most likely landscape behaviour to actually appear because it's only two steps and the payoff is close. Weeks 3-4. Genuinely satisfying.

2. A crop. High yield, low poison, seeds that no longer scatter, and thirstier than its wild cousins because it only ever gets replanted on damp ground near camp. Month 3. This is the flagship result and it will land.

3. A second crop. Same thing again on a different plant species. Month 4. It's real, and it feels like a rerun, because it is one — same mechanism, different sprite.

4. Nutrient exhaustion rings and camp relocation. The soil numbers near a long-lived camp go to zero and the tribe moves. It reads like a story about depleted land. It is a number hitting zero.

5. The crop collapse. Yield bred up, poison bred down, pest arrives, harvest gone. Maybe 50/50 that your parameters ever let it fire. If it does, it's the highlight of the six months.

6. Tamer animals. The "flee distance" dial dropping inside herded groups — tameness, evolved, not coded. Depends on HERD working, which is another multi-step problem, so call it a coin flip.

7. Six to ten "recurring patterns" flagged by the pattern-finder, of which about three are actually distinct and the rest are old shapes rotated or scaled. You'll stop reading these alerts around month 4.

8. Only if you build the shelf of pre-made moves: channels, a dam, terraces on a slope, and a fight over who's upstream. That's items 8 through 11 and they're the ones you'd actually show someone. They arrive because you handed the AI a "dig a line" button, not because it worked out lines from scratch.
projections.reaches_technology:
No. Not close, and the design's own author says so in the honest-ceiling section — the audit just says it more sharply.

Take the chain one link at a time. Cavemen: yes, you get small tribes foraging and starving. Fire: yes, genuinely, and it's one of the better results — burn-then-plant shows up on its own in week 3 or 4. Houses: no. There is no building in this world. FENCE is the nearest thing and it's a wall of squares. Tools: no. There is no material anywhere in the simulation — no wood you can shape, no stone, no way to combine two things into a third thing. Technology: there is no path at all. The doc admits there's "no channel for materials or mechanisms," which is the polite way of saying the eight verbs are a hard wall. Add a ninth verb and you get one more direction. That's the only lever, and pulling it is you inventing, not the world.

So the ceiling is roughly: fire management, some breeding, and — if you build the shortcut layer — some digging. The audit's judgement is that only the breeding half is safe, and the digging half is at serious risk of never arriving.

Is the civilization framing a costume? Mostly, yes, and I'd rather say it straight. This is not a project about a civilization inventing things. It's an ecology-and-evolution simulator, a very good one, in which the agents are mainly a selection pressure applied to the plants. The plants are the ones doing the evolving. The tribes are the weather that shapes them. "The tech tree is written into the terrain and you can read it from orbit" is a lovely sentence, and the terrain part is real — but there are six to ten shapes in that tech tree, most of them are burn patches, and by month 6 you'll be able to recite them. If you'd be happy building a world where the AI never really builds anything and the wildlife is the star, this is an excellent project. If you want to watch something get cleverer over time, this isn't it, and the disappointment will arrive in month 2.
projections.honest_month6_feeling:
Week 2 you refresh it at traffic lights. Month 6 you glance at it while the kettle boils, and some mornings you forget.

That's partly by design and not a failure — the whole point of the wall-mounted display is that the world changes slowly, and a slow world means most mornings nothing new happened. But you should know what "nothing new" actually feels like after 120 mornings in a row.

Here's where your time actually goes by month 6. Three things, none of them glamorous.

First, tuning the ecology. The doc admits this and the audit underlines it: an unbalanced world either goes extinct in week one or fills up solid by week two, and getting the numbers into a band that stays interesting for months is fiddly work that no paper will do for you. You will spend weeks on it and you will redo it every time you change a verb.

Second, fighting the water. The audit is blunt here and it's the most concrete technical warning in the whole review. Water flowing across a big grid, done the simple way described, either blows up numerically or quietly leaks water out of the world without telling you. And that matters more than it sounds: the moisture numbers are the thing your headline domestication chart is measured against. If water is silently vanishing, your best result is measured against a broken ruler. The fix is boring — check that total water is conserved on every single tick, and shout if it isn't — but budget a week for it and don't skip it.

Third, the morning alerts. The design's alert system trains a small predictor on the world and pings you when its guess about tomorrow is badly wrong. The audit's verdict: that fires on rain, on random fire spread, and on the predictor's own retraining wobble, far more often than on anything real. You'll get paged every morning about weather. The correct thing to measure is different — whether the world became more predictable over time — and you'll end up rewriting it, probably in month 2 or 3, after two weeks of false alarms.

So: month 6, honestly, is you adjusting numbers, watching a slow map, and re-reading a chart that stopped moving in month 4. The world is beautiful and it is running. It is not surprising you very often. The new things it flags are mostly old things at a different angle with a new cluster ID.
projections.who_should_pick_it: Pick this if you'd genuinely enjoy building a living ecosystem for its own sake and would be content if the AI tribes never build a single thing — because the plants doing the evolving are the real star here, and the audit says the tribe-as-engineer half may never show up at all.
projections.jargon_decoder:
RASTER — a grid of squares, like a bitmap image, where every square stores a handful of numbers (height, water, nutrients) instead of a colour.

PPO — the standard trial-and-error training method: the agent acts, gets a score, and nudges its behaviour a little toward whatever scored better last time.

NICHE CONSTRUCTION — creatures changing the place they live, so the place then changes which creatures survive; here, tribes reshaping the land that feeds them, and the land shaping them back.

SPARSE-REWARD, LONG-HORIZON CREDIT ASSIGNMENT — the payoff arrives hundreds of steps after the useful action, so the learner has no way to work out which action earned it; this is the exact reason the digging half probably fails.

CFL-LIMITED — a hard speed limit on physics simulations: move water too far in one time step and the maths either explodes or quietly deletes water without warning you.

COMPRESSION PROGRESS (vs PREDICTION ERROR) — "is the world getting easier to predict over time?" is real news; "was tonight's guess wrong?" is usually just weather, and the design measures the second one by mistake.
projections.name: LOAM

projections.plain_pitch: You write a tiny fake computer in about 600 lines — you invent its instruction set, you write the loop that runs it. Then you write one small program that copies itself, drop it into a big block of memory, and let the copies mutate as they go. Every night a script stops the world, looks at all the programs still alive, finds the chunk of code they keep repeating, and turns that chunk into a single new instruction on your fake computer that runs cheaper than the long version. That's it. Six months of that and you have a list of subroutines the system found rather than you writing them, plus a lot of programs fighting over memory and stealing each other's fuel.
projections.how_it_invents_plain:
Here is one invention, start to finish.

Every program in the soup has to copy itself to survive. Copying means a loop: read a byte from here, write it there, move both pointers along, count down, jump back. On your fake computer that's maybe six instructions, fourteen bytes. Nearly every program that is still alive has that exact fourteen-byte run somewhere in it, because if you don't have it, you don't reproduce, so you're not there.

Night falls. The script dumps out every surviving program as a string of bytes and asks one question: which run of bytes shows up most often, weighted by how long it is? Same question zip asks about your file. It finds the fourteen-byte copy loop, 900 copies of it. It takes an unused instruction number — say 0x7A — and says: from now on, 0x7A means "run those fourteen bytes." And it makes 0x7A cost 9 fuel instead of 14. A small language model reads the log and calls it "Threadfast."

Your phone buzzes. You open it, tap the card, read the disassembly with coffee, and it's memcpy. You didn't write that. It found it. That moment is completely real and it happens in week one or two.

Now the part the pitch doesn't say out loud. What got minted is a *literal* run of bytes — the exact fourteen, with the exact register numbers and the exact offsets baked in. It has no blanks in it. It is a copy-pasted snippet, not a function you can call with different arguments. So a program can only use 0x7A if it wanted precisely those fourteen bytes, byte for byte. The design's whole headline argument is "each new instruction makes new programs reachable — one mutation now does what fourteen used to." That argument is only true for shortcuts that have *holes* in them: "copy N bytes from A to B" with N, A and B as slots. Snippets with no holes don't enlarge what's reachable. They just make one path you already walk slightly cheaper. The audit is blunt about this and it is the single most important thing in the document, because the fix is either (a) the change the audit recommends — compare pairs of good code fragments, spot where they differ, punch holes there — or (b) the route the design actually names, which means converting jumpy machine code back into neat nested expressions so a proper tool can chew on it. That's writing a decompiler. It is not a weekend. And it is quietly holding up the entire "this grows forever" section.
projections.month6_screen:
A square of coloured static, 512 by 512. Four or five big irregular blobs of colour with speckly borders, a couple of dark patches where the fuel ran out. It is genuinely pretty. It looks almost exactly like it looked three weeks ago. If you built the eight parallel worlds, there are eight of these and you have stopped looking at six of them.

Under it, three small line charts. Population: a flat sawtooth, same shape every week. Max depth of the invention family tree: 7. It was 7 last month. It was 6 in week nine. Distinct tribes alive: 5, down from 8, and it only goes down between collapses.

Under that, the Codex Diff card, which is the good bit of the design and does work: "Tribe 4 minted OP_C3 — Vethmarrow. 11 bytes. Gain 340. First used by wright #88213." You tap it. The disassembly is the parity routine followed by the store loop. You have read both of those before, separately, months ago. The family tree branch shows it hanging off two things you already know.

Above all of that, three notifications from last night, because you capped it at three. Two are "clade shift" — a lineage crossed 20% of the population — which mostly means a slightly different variant of the same winner took over. One is a genuine first-ever event signature, and when you look it up it's a parasite variant using a different entry offset.

Elsewhere in the room: a spike of receipt-printer paper with the nightly family tree on it. That object is lovely. That part of the pitch is true.
projections.month6_invented_examples:
These are the honest ones, not the good-day ones. I'll give the flavour name a small model would slap on it, then what it actually is.

Threadfast — the copy loop. Read, write, bump both pointers, count down, jump back. Every replicator needs it. Minted night one or two. Correct, boring, and the design admits it.

Kellmarrow — a bounded memcpy. Same as above but it stops at a length instead of running off the end. This is the week-two "oh, that's genuinely useful and nobody wrote it" one. Enjoy it, it's real.

Sunder-Tally — an accumulator loop. Walk a run of bytes, add them up, leave the total somewhere. It exists because a bounty pays for checksums.

Grey Ferrow — XOR everything in a stream together. One of your eight authored transforms, solved.

Ashcount — count the odd bits. Parity. Another of your eight.

Vethmarrow — Sunder-Tally followed by Grey Ferrow. Two things it already had, glued in a fixed order, because a bounty asked for "do f then g" and composition was one of the operators you handed it. From here on, most new mints look like this. Real code, minted honestly, but it is a pair of old things with a new name on it. The family tree gets deeper. It does not get wider.

Hollowgate — the parasite's move: jump into a neighbour's code and run on the neighbour's fuel. Emerges around month two, no bounty required, and it is the most alive-feeling thing in the whole project.

Warden's Seam — a checksum guard on the entry point, so a program refuses to run if its own code has been tampered with. Immunity. It arrives because parasites arrived. This is the best content the system produces and it is also exactly where Tierra got to in 1991 and then stopped.

What is not on this list, at any point, in any world: anything you would call a house, a fire, a hammer, a farm, or a wheel.
projections.reaches_technology:
No. Not close. Not in a soft "it's an abstract version of that" way — it does not reach it in principle, and you should hear that clearly before you spend a weekend on it.

The civilization framing is a costume, and the audit says so directly: "the phone view will read as a civilization while the substrate is a list of machine instructions." Translate that. A "tribe" is a group of byte-strings that happen to share the same lookup table of shortcuts. A "war" is one program overwriting another program's memory. "Trade" is copying a row of a lookup table across and charging fuel for it. A "dark age" is you tapping a button to freeze a lookup table. And the "technology" your phone announces at 3am is a bounded memcpy with a fantasy name that a 4-billion-parameter language model made up after reading a JSON log. Nothing about the naming is grounded in anything. The model is a flavour-text generator sitting on top of a compression dictionary. That is the entire civilization layer.

There is no fire because there is no heat, no matter, no space in any physical sense, and no body. There is a byte array and a fuel counter. The one honest word in the whole design for what it produces is in its own ceiling section: "a self-authored tech tree of computational primitives." That is the real endpoint. Subroutines. Good ones, found not written, in a family tree you didn't draw — but subroutines.

And on how far even that goes, the design and the audit disagree, and you should believe the audit. Design says a plateau at month three or four, family-tree depth 6-10. Audit says two hard stops, both earlier. First, week two to four: the script mines the programs that are still alive, but selection means the survivors are near-identical copies of whoever is winning. So "the most-repeated chunk" is just the champion's own body. It mints the champion as an instruction, that makes the champion cheaper to run, so the champion wins harder, so the population gets even more identical, so tomorrow it mints more of the champion. It is a feedback loop that pays for conformity and quietly kills the search. Second, week six to ten: the eight stream transforms are the actual content, and you wrote them. Once the shortcut table has an entry for each of the eight, every "do f then g" bounty is one or two mutations away by construction, because you handed it composition as a primitive. New mints stop being new kinds of thing. Depth 5 and beyond is "parity-thing then delta-thing."

One more. The design's own wildest ending — a program that runs the librarian on itself, from inside the world — is rated 20% by the pitch and 3% by the audit, and the audit is obviously right for a boring reason: the librarian is a batch script that runs outside the world at night. There is no instruction a program could execute to call it. For that ending to happen you would have to build it yourself, which means it isn't emergent, which means it isn't the thing you wanted.
projections.honest_month6_feeling:
Week two, checking it is electric. There is a specific feeling — your phone tells you the name of a subroutine, you read the disassembly, and it's a real piece of code that you did not write and could not have predicted the exact bytes of. Nobody can take that off you and it is worth the weekend on its own.

Month six, checking it feels like glancing at a long-running build. Ten seconds. The picture looks the same. The depth number hasn't moved in nine weeks. You read the new instruction, recognise both halves of it, and put the phone down. The notifications have quietly become a thing you dismiss rather than a thing you open.

The bigger shift is what you're *doing*. By month six you are not adding features. You are tuning: the fuel cost table, the size of the discount, how many shortcut slots each tribe gets, how aggressively the eviction rule throws old ones out. Then you add a ninth stream transform to the bounty list to try to kick it off the plateau, and you get two good weeks, and then it flattens again at the new level. Then you consider a tenth. That is the loop you are actually in.

Notice what that means. The invention has moved. In week two the system was doing something surprising. By month six *you* are the source of new content, and the system is a very fast, very honest machine for solving whatever you last put in front of it. Its own document says this in a nicer voice — "you will be tuning the cycle cost model and the task grammar, not writing new features, which is either heaven or boredom depending on your temperament." That's fair, and there really are people for whom it's heaven. But be honest with yourself about which one you are, because the sentence is doing a lot of work.

One genuinely warm thing: because everything is denominated in fake fuel rather than wall-clock time, and there's a full log with a fixed random seed, any night replays exactly. You can go back to night 40 and step through it. That's proper engineering and it's the best-built thing in the batch. It will make debugging at month six pleasant rather than maddening.
projections.best_moment: Sunday night of the first weekend, or week two at the latest. You've got a 32-instruction fake computer running over a 4MB block of memory, drawn to a canvas at 10fps — this is a JS project, typed arrays and a canvas, exactly your wheelhouse. You watch your hand-written self-copier take over the whole soup and then, unprompted, get *shorter*, because short programs pay less fuel. That alone is a great Saturday. Then Sunday you write the crude nightly script, it finds the copy loop, mints it, and your phone tells you the name of a thing you did not write. The delight moment lands early and it lands reliably. The problem is not the first moment. It is the fifth month.
projections.worst_moment:
Week two to four, and it is nasty because it looks like success. The system is minting new instructions every night. The notifications are coming. The family tree is growing. And what is actually happening is that the nightly script is looking at a population of near-clones and minting the winner's own body, over and over, in bigger and bigger pieces — then handing the winner a discount, which makes it win harder, which makes the clones more identical, which makes tomorrow's mint even more of the same. You will not spot this from the dashboard. You'll spot it when you finally read four consecutive nights of disassembly and realise they're overlapping slices of one organism. That is a demoralising afternoon, and the fix (mine each family separately, score a shortcut by how many *unrelated* lineages use it, not raw count) is real work.

The second worst moment is week six to ten and it's quieter: the plateau. You add a ninth transform to the bounty list, get a fortnight of movement, and watch it flatten. That's the one where you find out whether the tuning loop is heaven or boredom for you.
projections.who_should_pick_it: Pick this if you are in love with the substrate — building a tiny CPU and watching programs fight, steal fuel and evolve immune systems inside it — and not with the story on top of it; if you want cavemen and fire, this will disappoint you within a month and you should walk away now.
projections.jargon_decoder:
OPCODE — one byte that means one instruction on the fake computer you wrote. There are 256 possible values; half are the instructions you defined, half are left empty for the ones the system invents.

BYTECODE / GENOME — the creature *is* its program. A "wright" is just a run of bytes, each byte an instruction, plus a pointer to where it's up to and a fuel counter. Nothing else. When the doc says genome it means that string of bytes.

ISA — the complete list of instructions your fake computer understands. The whole headline of the project is that this list grows on its own.

MDL — "the best explanation is the shortest one." In practice here: find the repeated chunk of bytes that saves the most space if you give it a single-byte name. Same question a zip file asks.

WAKE/SLEEP (from a project called DreamCoder) — run the world all day, then stop at night and compress what worked into shortcuts. It is a batch script that runs outside the world, which matters: nothing inside the world can call it.

S-EXPRESSION IR / STITCH — Stitch is a real tool that finds shortcuts *with blanks in them* ("copy N bytes from A to B"), which is the only kind that actually makes new programs reachable. But it needs code written as neat nested brackets, and yours is flat machine code full of jumps. Converting one to the other is writing a decompiler. The design mentions this in passing; it is actually the load-bearing step of the whole pitch.

NICHE CONSTRUCTION — "the thing reshapes the world it lives in." Here it means inventing a shortcut changes what a single mutation can reach. The audit's verdict: true only for shortcuts with blanks, false for the copy-paste snippets the cheap version actually produces.

One last thing worth knowing: the document cites a 2026 Sakana AI paper with a full conference DOI. The audit flags it as the most likely fabricated reference in the entire batch. Don't cite it to anyone until you've personally loaded the URL.
projections.name: Cinderloom

diag.what_he_actually_wants:
He wants to wake up, look at his phone, and see that a PLACE got more built overnight without him. Not a document, not a dashboard, not a portfolio of twelve worlds — a place, with objects in it, that he can point at and say "that wasn't there last week and I didn't put it there."

Two things back that up. He chose the check-in where the new thing is a specific object at a specific spot with a date on it. And three of his four picks are engines that give things NAMES. He probably wouldn't say out loud that the naming matters, but it's in the picks.

He also wants to be able to open the hood and understand the whole machine. That's why every design where a language model makes the actual calls got binned. He isn't chasing open-ended technology. He's chasing a legible world that grows.
diag.common_thread:
Look at what he threw away, not just what he kept. Three entire families got wiped out — every single member, no survivors. That's not noise.

**1. Anything where a language model decides what happens.** Roughly ten of the 42 work like this: the tribe combines two things, a model is asked "what does this become?", and the answer is cached forever. The Slow Kiln (both copies), THE KILN, Grist, The Ninefold Constitution, The Ninefold Gazette, The Ark of Constants, The Dreaming Stone, Ninety-Nine Anvils. Gone, all of them.

In his four, the referee is always code you could step through in a debugger. A little machine runs a program and counts the steps (Ashcairn, Glyphworks). A processor runs instructions and charges for them (Cinderloom). Water flows downhill and plants that got eaten don't get to breed (LOAM). The language model is only ever allowed to pick names. That is the single biggest split in the whole pool and he landed on the right side of it — I suspect without being able to say why.

**2. Anything where the morning payoff is a piece of writing.** Eleven-plus designs hand you a newspaper, a scripture, an encyclopedia, a museum label, an excavation report, a dictionary, a critical edition, a scientific paper. Marginalia, Apocrypha, Palimpsest, Scriptorium, Strata, Reliquary, Psalmdrift, The Telling, Saltmark, Bureau of Comparative Worlds. All gone.

In his four, the morning thing is either a picture of a place (a valley, a landscape, a block of memory) or a piece of code short enough to read. Things you can *check*. A nice paragraph written by a small model can't be wrong, and he smelled that.

**3. Anything that's a dashboard of a dozen worlds side by side.** Nine tribes in a 3x3 grid, twelve planets, thirty-two worlds, eight soups, a portfolio of civilizations to compare. All gone. All four of his are one place that keeps its own history.

**The positive version, in one line:** he picked the four you could explain to a programmer over a pint without using a single word from a paper, and where the payoff is a specific object rather than a feeling.

Test it:

- **Ashcairn** — at night, something reads all the code that worked yesterday, finds a chunk that keeps repeating, and pulls it out into a named function. That named function IS a technology. He's a JS dev. That's refactoring. He does it every week.
- **Glyphworks** — same, but that named function can be turned into a building standing at one spot on the map, and afterwards it's cheap only there.
- **Cinderloom** — same, but the code is raw machine instructions, and the repeated chunk becomes a new single instruction that costs less to run.
- **LOAM** — no naming at all. The tribe eats the tastiest plants and replants the seeds it was carrying, so a few hundred plant generations later the plants near the tribe really are tastier. Digging moves water. That's the whole thing.

Four mechanisms, four sentences, no vocabulary. Almost none of the other 38 can be stated that way. Sandwright needs "an archive that keeps the single best example of each kind of behaviour". Winterforge needs "a level editor trained to make the tribe fail as badly as possible". The Telling needs "a language becoming compositional under a teaching bottleneck". Those might be better ideas. They are not *statable* ideas, for him, today.

Two more things worth noticing, and both are uncomfortable.

**His filter was partly a readability filter, and how readable a pitch is has roughly nothing to do with how good the design is.** LOAM has the plainest English of all 42. It also scored 7.3 in the pool's own ranking, below four ideas he couldn't parse. Being understandable got LOAM into his shortlist. That's a warning, not a recommendation. More on that next.

**Three of the four have a genuinely great first weekend written into the document. Glyphworks doesn't, and admits it:** "weekend one is honestly Emberlisp's weekend; this idea's distinctive part needs that substrate underneath." Hold that thought — it's the whole answer to the overlap question.
diag.wrong_reason_pick:
**LOAM. Not close.**

The last line of the pitch is "the tech tree is written into the terrain and you can read it from orbit." That's the sentence that sold it. It's also the half of the design that probably never happens.

Split LOAM in two.

**Half one — the plants and animals. This works.** It is the most honest mechanism in all 42 documents. The tribe prefers plants that taste better and carries their seeds around, so those are the plants that get to breed, so a few hundred plant generations later the plants growing on tribe land have higher yield, less poison, and hold onto their seeds instead of scattering them. That is literally what happened to wheat, and it requires no cleverness from the agents at all — only a preference. You get a chart out of it: average yield number for plants inside tribe territory versus outside, two lines pulling apart over months. That chart is real, it cannot be faked, and it lands around month three.

**Half two — the digging and burning. This is the part that gives you the landscape you can read from orbit. Channels, terraces, dams. And it's a known-hard learning problem, not a tuning problem.**

Here's why in plain terms. For an irrigation channel to pay off you have to dig twenty tiles in a row and then wait three hundred ticks for water to show up. A channel that's five tiles long is strictly *worse* than never digging — you burned the energy and got nothing. So every step toward the thing that would help gets punished. Nothing gets better as you get closer. The learn-by-reward method LOAM plans to use is famously beaten by exactly this shape; the Craftax benchmark exists to demonstrate it, and the multi-agent follow-up paper that LOAM itself cites concludes that all the standard methods fail at problems shaped like this. **The design cites the papers that say its plan won't work.**

The proposed fix is to hand-write a few construction routines — "dig a line of length n downhill", "burn this patch then come back" — and let the search pick which one and with what numbers. That does work. It also means *you drew the shape of the channel and the sim picked its length*. The unauthored quality that made LOAM attractive quietly dies right there.

**So the mismatch, precisely: the pitch promises a built landscape and delivers an evolved ecosystem.** Both are lovely. They are not the same product. Month six of LOAM is most likely a gorgeous, slowly shifting map of burn scars, moisture and forest turning to grass — genuinely beautiful, honestly a very good screensaver — plus two or three charts that prove something real about domestication, plus no channels, no terraces, and nothing that ever gets a name.

**And here's the bit that should decide it.** He just told us his favourite check-in is "a kiln appeared where there wasn't one, the tribe built it themselves, and the settlement is clustering around it." **LOAM cannot produce that sentence.** Nothing in LOAM is discrete. Nothing *appears*. The map changes by smearing — the moisture is a bit different, that patch is a bit greener. There is no event to push to his phone. He picked a design whose most likely output is the wrong *shape* for the check-in he says he wants.

**Runner-up, briefly: Cinderloom.** Its pitch says "civilizations". There are no civilizations in it and there never will be. The technologies it discovers are things like "copy twelve bytes and add one", and the only thing making them sound civilizational is a small local model writing captions over them. That's fine and honest work *if* what he wants is a processor that evolves its own instruction set, which is a genuinely cool thing to want. But if he read "civilizations" and pictured anything at all, he mis-read it.

There's a second, quieter Cinderloom problem worth naming, because it's the same trick the pitch turns on. Its nightly compressor as described finds repeated *literal* byte-strings — no slots, no arguments, no variables. A chunk with no arguments doesn't open up new programs; it just makes one existing path shorter. The pitch's big claim — "each new instruction enlarges what's reachable" — is only true for the harder version with slots in it, which requires turning flat machine code with arbitrary jumps back into a tree structure first. That's writing a decompiler. It is not the weekend project the doc implies, and it's quietly holding up the entire argument.
diag.overlaps:
**Yes. Two of the four are the same project, and it's stated in the documents — this isn't a judgment call.**

**Glyphworks is Ashcairn plus one feature.**

Ashcairn and Emberlisp (which he didn't pick) are near-twins: a small valley, a tiny language the agents act in, and a nightly pass that finds repeated chunks in the programs that worked and pulls them out as named functions. Glyphworks says outright that its world is "identical in spirit to Emberlisp", and its own first-weekend section says: *"Weekend one is honestly Emberlisp's weekend; this idea's distinctive part needs that substrate underneath."*

Their tech stacks are the same line for line — same compressor library, same database, same local model doing the naming, same push notifications, same web page. Glyphworks' tech section literally opens with "Emberlisp's stack plus: a works table…".

**So this is not two projects. It's month one and month two of one project.** Build the little language, the search, and the nightly compressor — that's Ashcairn, and that's where the first surprise lives (Sunday afternoon of weekend one). Then add the rule: a named function that always runs at one spot and is expensive gets built as a *building* at that spot, and afterwards it's cheap there. That's Glyphworks. Same codebase, one new table and one change to how the search costs things.

**Two things Ashcairn owns that Glyphworks doesn't mention, both cheap, both worth stealing:**

- **The teaching limit.** A tribe can only pass on a handful of functions per season, so a big pile of knowledge is a *liability* for a small band, and tribes that keep their knowledge small and well-organised beat the hoarders. That's a genuinely counter-intuitive thing to watch and it's maybe fifty lines of code.
- **The transplant test.** Carry one function to a differently-generated valley and see if it still works. Survives = it was a real law. Dies = it was a local trick. That's a free, honest measure of whether an invention was ever real, computed by the sim on itself, every night.

**Cinderloom is not a superset or a subset — it's the same loop one floor down.** Same nightly idea: find a repeated chunk in whatever survived, give it a name, make it cheaper to run. The difference is there's no world in it. No valley, no people, no map. The programs live in a big block of memory and eat processor time.

**So the real headline for him: of his four picks, three are the same engine wearing different clothes, and one (LOAM) is a genuinely different project.** He hasn't picked four things. He's picked one thing, three times, and one alternative. That's actually good news — it means the decision in front of him is much smaller than it looks.
diag.ai_writes_code_implications:
It changes less than it feels like it changes, and it changes things in an order that matters.

**What it genuinely removes:** "I don't know Rust", "I've never touched JAX", "I've never used a compressor library." Gone. Real, and it matters — it's the reason Glyphworks stops being unreasonable. Glyphworks' own honest ceiling says the first month is building search machinery rather than watching a world. If someone else types that month, that objection is dead.

**What it does not remove, in increasing order of nastiness:**

**1. Tuning.** Every one of the four says this in its own words.
