LOAM: *"an unbalanced biota either goes extinct in week 1 or fills everything by week 2, and getting the parameters into a regime that stays interesting for months is real fiddly work no paper will do for you."* Glyphworks: the rule that decides which functions become buildings *"will need tuning a few times in the first month — too loose and the map fills with junk buildings, too tight and nothing gets built."* Cinderloom's own six-months-later: *"You will be tuning the cycle cost model and the task grammar, not writing new features — which is either heaven or boredom depending on your temperament."* No coding help touches this. It's taste, applied one number at a time, at night, for months.

**2. Debugging, and specifically the worst kind of debugging.** Glyphworks' hard part is a cache-invalidation problem. The search remembers "I already tried this program, here's what it did" so it doesn't redo work. But now what a program does depends on which buildings are within reach — and buildings get built and fall down. Key that memory wrong and the search silently reuses an answer from a world that no longer exists. Nothing crashes. There's no error. You get a tribe solving something it shouldn't be able to solve, and you find out three weeks later when the map looks wrong.

An AI writing code produces that class of bug *faster*, not slower, and he's the one who has to smell it. Make the fix a day-one requirement, not a later cleanup: stamp every site with a version number that bumps whenever a building goes up or falls down, and treat every remembered answer as valid only for its own version number. That one line is the difference between a debuggable project and a haunted one.

**3. Speed.** Ashcairn/Glyphworks' search has to try millions of candidate programs a night, and each try means running a little world forward. The audit is blunt: a Python version gives you maybe low millions per core per night when you need ten times that, and the doc's "port it to a fast language only if profiling demands it" is wrong — profiling demands it in week one. Fine, the AI writes the fast version. But it means the honest first milestone isn't "watch a civilization", it's "make the search fast enough to be worth watching". That's systems work, not design work.

**4. The one it truly cannot touch: content.** If the genuinely new things run out at week eight, writing code four times faster means he reaches week eight in three weeks. **Faster building brings the plateau forward. It does not raise it.** Every audit in the set independently names the same bottleneck, and it isn't the compressor and it isn't the search — it's the supply of new problems for the tribe to solve. That's a design problem. Design is his job, not the AI's.

**Given all that, the ranking shifts:**

- **LOAM is helped least.** Its blocker is a real research problem — getting a learner to dig a twenty-tile channel when nineteen tiles is worse than zero. No amount of coding help solves that, and the only known fix half-authors the thing he wanted unauthored.
- **Cinderloom is helped moderately.** Its hard part is turning flat machine instructions back into a tree so the compressor can find chunks with slots in them. That's real engineering, which is exactly what an AI is good at. So the version of Cinderloom that actually compounds becomes buildable, where before it wasn't.
- **Glyphworks is helped most.** Its blocker is labour plus systems, which is what the help is for — and it's the only one of the four that produces the check-in he chose.

But "helped most" and "safest" are different words. Glyphworks is the highest-variance of the four, and the variance is concentrated in silent-wrong-answer bugs during a month when he isn't yet getting any payoff for putting up with them.
diag.the_one_decision:
**First, kill the question he's stuck on.**

"Does it matter if the sim never reaches real technology?" — it will never reach real technology. Not one of the 42. No metal, no machines, no steam, ever. LOAM's own document says "the neolithic, and that is it." Glyphworks gets three to five stacked storeys of building and then sprawls sideways. Cinderloom's technologies are ways of copying bytes around. Ashcairn tops out at maybe 30-80 named functions, four deep. Anyone answering that question with a yes is selling.

So stop weighting it. It has the same answer for every candidate, so it decides nothing.

---

**Here's the question that actually decides something, and he has to answer it before a line is written:**

# Does the new thing need a NAME?

That's the fork. It's the only real one among his four.

**Branch A — yes, it needs a name.**

Then every morning the app has a definite answer to "did anything happen": either something got minted last night or it didn't. You can read its body. It has a birth date, a list of parents, and a count of how many times it's been used since. When the compressor pulls out a chunk you never wrote and the small local model calls it `bank-the-coals`, that's the jolt — and it's the most reliable jolt in the whole pool, because it arrives on the first Sunday afternoon rather than in month three.

This means: **build Ashcairn's engine, then bolt Glyphworks' buildings onto it. One project.** Drop LOAM. Drop Cinderloom unless he'd rather have a beautiful CPU toy than a valley — in which case it's a fine, much simpler standalone thing he could run in parallel without it costing him anything.

**Branch B — no, a changed picture is enough.**

Then build LOAM, and go in knowing exactly what he's getting: an ecosystem that's hypnotic by the first Saturday night, a genuine and unfakeable domestication chart by month three, and probably no channels, no terraces, no buildings, ever. Nothing gets named. No notification is worth reading, because nothing discrete ever happens. The reward is looking, not reading.

---

**His own answers already vote for Branch A, twice.**

He chose Glyphworks' check-in: a kiln appeared where there wasn't one, the tribe built it, the settlement is clustering around it, scrub six months of history. Every clause of that needs discrete, named, dated objects with locations. And three of his four picks are the naming engine anyway.

So the honest recommendation is Branch A. One project. Ashcairn's engine in month one, Glyphworks' buildings in month two, steal the teaching limit and the transplant test as cheap extras.

---

**But don't take my word for it — settle the fork in a weekend, because his gut is better evidence than my reasoning.**

**The test.** Build the Ashcairn/Emberlisp weekend, which with an AI typing is more like a day. A tiny language with about forty commands. A world small enough to be boring. One brute-force search over programs that keeps an agent from freezing overnight. Then feed every program that worked into the compressor, print the top repeated chunk it found and how much space it saved, add it to the language as a new command, re-run the search, and watch the same problem solve in a fraction of the tries.

If that Sunday afternoon gives him a jolt — if reading a function he didn't write, that his own tribe carved out of its own behaviour, actually *feels* like something — he's Branch A. Commit to Glyphworks and stop reading design documents.

If he shrugs — if his honest reaction is "okay, it deduplicated some code" — then nothing built on top will fix that, and he should build LOAM and enjoy the map.

---

**And the last honest thing, month six of Branch A, since he asked and since the boring part is what decides whether this is a year of good coffee or a shelf project.**

The valley has maybe 60-100 buildings, in five to eight *kinds*. The library has 80-150 named functions, four to six layers deep — not the 300-800 the document promises. Three nights out of four the notification says a new function was minted, and when he taps it, the body is two things he already had, stuck together, wearing a name that a 4-billion-parameter model wrote. **The name is the most impressive part of it, and the name is the part that's fake.** Most nights the map gets busier without getting different. His evenings go on moving numbers: how much saving before something earns a name, how expensive before it becomes a building, how often the river floods.

That's the truth, and it's most of month six.

**What's still genuinely good at month six:** the time-lapse. Six months of a valley filling up, a flood taking out the lower works, and the rebuild going a *different route* than the original — that is real, it's his, nobody wrote it, and it's the best thing to show another human out of any of the 42. The map is also its own lie detector: a field of buildings nobody ever uses is *obviously* a bug, whereas a list of ninety named functions looks like success. That's a real design virtue and it's exactly why Glyphworks beats its own siblings.

**And maybe once or twice in six months, the good one:** a building that can only be made from a material that another building produces. That's the moment craft becomes industry, and it's the only genuinely unpredictable event on the table.

It might not happen. That's the bet. He should place it knowing that's the bet.
